claim: Propofol acts by enhancing GABAergic inhibition throughout the brain and central nervous system.
source: Propofol – the most widely used anesthetic – acts by enhancing GABAergic inhibition throughout the brain and central nervous system (Bai et al., 1999; Hapfelmeier et al., 2001; Hemmings et al., 2019; Hemmings et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research (Bai et al., 1999; Hapfelmeier et al., 2001; Hemmings et al., 2019; Hemmings et al., 2005).

claim: At low doses, propofol produces a sedative state associated with beta oscillations (13–25 Hz).
source: At low doses, propofol produces a sedative state associated with beta oscillations (13–25 Hz) (McCarthy et al., 2008; Purdon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (McCarthy et al., 2008; Purdon et al., 2015).

claim: At higher doses that maintain unconsciousness for surgery, slow-delta oscillations (0.1–4 Hz) appear across the entire scalp and are decoupled between cortical regions.
source: At higher doses that maintain unconsciousness for surgery, slow-delta oscillations (0.1–4 Hz) (Lewis et al., 2012; McCarley, 2007) appear across the entire scalp and are decoupled between cortical regions (Lewis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lewis et al., 2012; McCarley, 2007).

claim: Coherent alpha oscillations (8–12 Hz) concentrate across the frontal area of the scalp during propofol-induced unconsciousness, a process known as anteriorization.
source: Concomitantly, coherent alpha oscillations (8–12 Hz) concentrate across the frontal area of the scalp, a process known as anteriorization (Cimenser et al., 2011; Purdon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Cimenser et al., 2011; Purdon et al., 2013).

claim: In profound states of propofol-induced unconsciousness, the phase of the slow-delta oscillations strongly modulates the amplitude of the alpha oscillations.
source: In profound states of propofol-induced unconsciousness, the phase of the slow-delta oscillations strongly modulates the amplitude of the alpha oscillations (Purdon et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Purdon et al., 2013).

claim: Unconsciousness is caused by the phase-locking of neuronal spiking with the slow-delta oscillation, which greatly reduces cortical spiking and limits cortical activity to brief Up-states of spiking followed by longer duration Down-states of little or no spiking.
source: One factor is that unconsciousness is caused by the phase-locking of neuronal spiking with the slow-delta oscillation. This greatly reduces cortical spiking and limits cortical activity to brief Up-states of spiking followed by longer duration Down-states of little or no spiking (Lewis et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lewis et al., 2012).

claim: The slow-delta oscillations 'fragment' the cortex by limiting local spiking to narrow windows of slow-delta oscillation phases, which being decoupled across cortical areas, impede long-range cortical communication.
source: Another factor is that the slow-delta oscillations 'fragment' the cortex (Lewis et al., 2012). Local spiking becomes limited to the narrow window of slow-delta oscillation phases, which being decoupled across cortical areas, impede long-range cortical communication.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lewis et al., 2012) and logical inference from the described mechanism.

claim: The coherent frontal alpha oscillations represent hypersynchronous communication between the thalamus and prefrontal cortex.
source: A third factor, supported by modeling and experimental studies, suggests that the coherent frontal alpha oscillations represent hypersynchronous communication between the thalamus and prefrontal cortex (Ching et al., 2010; Flores et al., 2017; Palva and Palva, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling and experimental studies (Ching et al., 2010; Flores et al., 2017; Palva and Palva, 2007).

claim: Unconsciousness is linked to loss of frontal-parietal connectivity.
source: A fourth factor links unconsciousness to loss of frontal-parietal connectivity (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lee et al., 2013).

claim: Direct action of propofol at GABAergic inhibitory synapses onto the arousal center nuclei in the brainstem is an important contributor to propofol-induced unconsciousness.
source: Finally, the neuroanatomy of the brainstem suggests that direct action of propofol at GABAergic inhibitory synapses onto the arousal center nuclei is also an important contributor to propofol-induced unconsciousness (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Brown et al., 2010) and knowledge of brainstem neuroanatomy.

claim: The thalamus is highly interconnected with the cortex and receives important inputs from the brainstem arousal centers.
source: The thalamus is highly interconnected with the cortex and receives important inputs from the brainstem arousal centers (Jones, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Jones, 2007).

claim: Thalamo-cortical and cortico-thalamic connectivity are highly layer specific.
source: Furthermore, both thalamo-cortical and cortico-thalamic connectivity are highly layer specific, giving rise to specific hypotheses that propose either deep (layers 5/6) or superficial (layer 2/3) may be more specifically linked to loss of consciousness (Aru et al., 2019; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Aru et al., 2019; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).

claim: Consciousness is linked more to frontal vs. posterior cortex.
source: Dehaene and Changeux, 2011 and others link consciousness more to frontal vs. posterior cortex (Boly et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Boly et al., 2017).

claim: Central thalamic stimulation can result in a partial restoration of consciousness.
source: Central thalamic stimulation can result in a partial restoration of consciousness (Schiff et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schiff et al., 2007).

claim: Some theories suggest consciousness is formed when oscillations in thalamo-cortical loops integrate cortical information.
source: Some theories suggest consciousness is formed when oscillations in thalamo-cortical loops integrate cortical information (Llinás, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Llinás, 2003).

claim: The thalamus regulates cortical communication (especially top-down) via oscillatory dynamics.
source: There is mounting evidence that the thalamus regulates cortical communication (especially top-down) via oscillatory dynamics (Halassa and Sherman, 2019; Saalmann and Kastner, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Halassa and Sherman, 2019; Saalmann and Kastner, 2015).

claim: Loss of consciousness (LOC) was associated with a significant decrease in muscle tone from 4.5 to 75 min after propofol infusion.
source: Relative to the Awake state, we observed a significant decrease in muscle tone (from 4.5 to 75 min, Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and statistical analysis (posterior probability > 0.99).

claim: Loss of consciousness (LOC) was associated with cessation of airpuff-evoked eyeblinks from 1 to 75 min after propofol infusion.
source: cessation of airpuff-evoked eyeblinks (from 1 to 75 min, Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and statistical analysis (posterior probability > 0.99).

claim: Loss of consciousness (LOC) was associated with a decline in blood oxygenation from 4.5 to 34 min after propofol infusion.
source: a decline in blood oxygenation (from 4.5 to 34 min, Figure 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis (posterior probability > 0.99).

claim: Loss of consciousness (LOC) was associated with a decrease in heart rate from 4.5 to 75 min after propofol infusion.
source: a decrease in heart rate (from 4.5 to 75 min, Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and statistical analysis (posterior probability > 0.99).

claim: Recovery of consciousness (ROC) occurred approximately 7 minutes after cessation of propofol infusion.
source: Once the infusion was ceased, ROC occurred in ~7 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 3–7 min before LOC, there was an increase in beta power in all cortical areas (~15–30 Hz).
source: First, approximately 3–7 min before LOC, there was an increase in beta power in all areas (~15–30 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2 with statistical significance (p<0.01, non-parametric cluster-based randomizations).

claim: In frontal areas PFC and 8A, beta power shifted to a lower frequency (~14–20 Hz) during the maintenance phase and remained higher than Awake throughout the Unconscious state.
source: In frontal areas PFC and 8A, this power change shifted to a lower frequency (~14–20 Hz) during the maintenance phase (Figure 2A and B, left subplots). Power in this frequency range remained higher than Awake throughout the Unconscious state.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: In posterior areas PPC and STG after LOC, beta power was reduced relative to Awake.
source: By contrast, in posterior areas PPC and STG after LOC (dotted black lines at time point 0 in Figure 2, left subplots) beta power was reduced relative to Awake (Figure 2C and D, left subplots).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: In all cortical areas, shortly before LOC there was a sustained reduction in gamma power (>35 Hz).
source: In all areas, shortly before LOC there was a sustained reduction in gamma power (>35 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: All cortical areas showed a significant increase in slow-frequency power around LOC.
source: All areas also showed a significant increase in slow-frequency power around LOC (Figure 2, non-parametric cluster-based randomizations, corrected for multiple comparisons; all effects p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: The strongest increase in slow-frequency power was seen in STG, then PPC/PFC, then 8A, organized from posterior to anterior.
source: The order of areas from strongest to weakest change was organized from posterior to anterior. The strongest increase in SF power was seen in STG, then PPC/PFC, then 8A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, significant differences in effect sizes were observed between STG and PFC and STG and 8A, p<0.01, non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: The thalamus showed an increase in slow frequency oscillations locked to LOC and a decrease in this same band locked to ROC.
source: There was an increase in slow frequency oscillations locked to LOC and a decrease in this same band locked to ROC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, p<0.01, non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: Area 8A showed a clear peak at 15 Hz during unconsciousness.
source: In particular, area 8A showed a clear peak at 15 Hz during unconsciousness (Figure 3A, red line).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: During the Awake state, alpha-beta (8–25 Hz) power in posterior areas, PPC and STG, was greater than in anterior areas, PFC and 8A.
source: We found that in the Awake state, alpha-beta (8–25 Hz) power in posterior areas, PPC and STG, was greater than in anterior areas, PFC and 8A (Figure 3B, sign test for anterior vs. posterior alpha-beta power across sessions, p<1E-3 for all comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis (p<1E-3).

claim: During the Unconscious state, alpha-beta power in frontal areas PFC and 8A was greater than in the posterior areas.
source: During the Unconscious state this relationship flipped. Alpha-beta power in frontal areas PFC and 8A was greater than in the posterior areas (Figure 3C, sign test for anterior vs. posterior alpha-beta power across sessions, p<1E-5 for all comparisons).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C with statistical analysis (p<1E-5).

claim: In anterior areas, PFC and 8A, the peak change in slow frequency was in higher frequencies (1.3 and 1.8 Hz, respectively) than posterior areas, PPC and STG (0.75 and 0.65 Hz, respectively).
source: In anterior areas, PFC and 8A, the peak change was in higher frequencies (Figure 3A, 1.3 and 1.8 Hz, respectively) than posterior areas, PPC and STG (Figure 3A, 0.75 and 0.65 Hz, respectively, sign test for frequency difference, all anterior vs. posterior comparisons, p<1E-5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis (p<1E-5).

claim: At ROC, power in the slow-frequency range was no longer significantly different from the Awake state in all areas.
source: In all areas, at ROC, power in the slow-frequency range was no longer significantly different from the Awake state (Figure 2A–D, right subpanels).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A–D (right subpanels).

claim: Significant reductions in gamma power were still present in PFC, 8A, and STG even 10 min post-ROC.
source: In contrast, significant reductions in gamma power were still present in PFC, 8A, and STG even 10 min post-ROC.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: In frontal area 8A, beta power remained elevated above Awake levels 10 min post-ROC.
source: In frontal area 8A, beta power remained elevated above Awake levels 10 min post-ROC (Figure 2B, right subpanel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B (right subpanel).

claim: In the Awake state, average spike rates were between 6 and 8 spikes per second across all areas.
source: In the Awake state, average spike rates were between 6 and 8 spikes per second across all areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: During the Unconscious state, average spike rates across areas fell to 0.2–0.5 spike/s during the initial infusion (first 30 min of propofol).
source: During the Unconscious state, average spike rates across areas fell to 0.2–0.5 spike/s during the initial infusion (first 30 min of propofol).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: During the maintenance infusion, spike rates increased to 1–2 spikes/s.
source: They increased to 1–2 spikes/s during the maintenance infusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At LOC, spike rates were approximately half of their Awake rates.
source: At LOC, spike rates were approximately half of their Awake rates (Figure 4A, mean firing rates at LOC: 4.0, 3.2, 3.4, 3.8 spikes/s for PFC, 8A, PPC, STG, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Spike rates stabilized ~15 min post-LOC to an average of 0.25 spikes/s.
source: Spike rates continued to fall and then stabilized ~15 min post-LOC to an average of 0.25 spikes/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At ROC, spiking activity increased to 3.3, 3.0, 3.4, and 5.0 spikes/s for PFC, 8A, PPC, STG, respectively, approximately the same spike rate as at LOC.
source: At ROC, spiking activity increased to 3.3, 3.0, 3.4, and 5.0 spikes/s (for PFC, 8A, PPC, STG, respectively), approximately the same spike rate as at LOC (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Area STG recovered faster than the other areas, with neurons having an average of 5.0 spikes/s at ROC, significantly greater than the other areas.
source: The exception was area STG, which recovered faster than the other areas. Neurons in STG had an average of 5.0 spikes/s at ROC, significantly greater than the other areas (p<0.01, non-parametric randomization test for all area comparisons to STG).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis with statistical testing (p<0.01).

claim: The strongest effects of spike rate reduction were in PFC/8A, then PPC, then STG, showing an anterior to posterior organization.
source: The order of areas from highest to lowest spike rate change showed an anterior to posterior organization. The strongest effects were in PFC/8A, then PPC, then STG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, all comparisons, p<0.01, non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: During the Unconscious state, spike timing was phase-coupled to the slow frequencies, appearing as Up and Down states of high vs. minimal to no spiking.
source: During the Unconscious state, spike timing was phase-coupled to the slow frequencies. This appeared as Up and Down states of high vs. minimal to no spiking, respectively (e.g., Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G and spike-triggered averages in Figure 4C/E/G/I.

claim: Spikes entrained to the depolarized phases (troughs) of slow frequency oscillations in all areas.
source: Spike-triggered averages of the LFP signal indicated that spikes entrained to the depolarized phases (troughs) of slow frequency oscillations (Figure 4C/E/G/I) in all areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C/E/G/I.

claim: The posterior probability of an increase in phase modulation during the Unconscious state was 0.99 for PFC, PPC, and 8A, and 0.98 for STG.
source: The posterior probability of an increase in phase modulation was 0.99 for PFC, PPC, and 8A, and 0.98 for STG.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using a beta-binomial model.

claim: Spiking and gamma reduction were more pronounced in superficial layers compared to deep layers.
source: Spiking and gamma reduction were more pronounced in superficial layers compared to deep layers (Figure 5B and D, non-parametric randomization test comparing the effect size of superficial vs. deep, p<1E-7 for spiking, p<1E-7 for gamma; Manly, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and D with statistical analysis (p<1E-7).

claim: The enhancement of slow frequency power was higher in deep compared to superficial layers.
source: The enhancement of slow frequency power was higher in deep compared to superficial layers (Figure 5F, non-parametric randomization test comparing the effect size of superficial vs. deep, p<1E-5 for SF).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F with statistical analysis (p<1E-5).

claim: There were strong increases in slow frequency cortico-cortical phase synchronization between all cortical areas during the Unconscious state.
source: There were strong increases in slow frequency cortico-cortical phase synchronization between all cortical areas (p<0.01, cluster-based non-parametric randomization test, Figure 6) during the Unconscious state.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: In a subset of area pairs, there were reductions in cortico-cortical theta and beta phase synchronization, although the effect size at these frequencies was smaller than at slow frequencies.
source: In a subset of area pairs (Figure 6B/E/F), there were reductions in cortico-cortical theta and beta phase synchronization, although the effect size at these frequencies was smaller than at slow frequencies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B/E/F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unique to phase synchronization between frontal areas PFC and 8A, there was a sustained increase in alpha (7–15 Hz) frequency range phase synchronization during the Unconscious state.
source: Unique to phase synchronization between frontal areas PFC and 8A, we observed a sustained increase in alpha (7–15 Hz) frequency range phase synchronization during the Unconscious state (p<0.01, cluster-based non-parametric randomization test, Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: During the Unconscious state, all cortical areas show increased slow frequency phase synchronization with the thalamus.
source: During the Unconscious state, all cortical areas show increased slow frequency phase synchronization with the thalamus (p<0.01, cluster-based non-parametric randomization test, Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7 with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: There were reductions in thalamo-cortical synchrony while Unconscious in the theta/beta frequency ranges, but these effects were smaller than slow-frequency effects.
source: There were also reductions in synchrony while Unconscious in the theta/beta frequency ranges, but as with cortico-cortical phase synchronization, these effects were smaller (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Uniquely to phase synchronization between thalamus and PFC, there was a sustained increase in alpha (7–15 Hz) frequency range phase synchrony while Unconscious.
source: Uniquely to phase synchronization between thalamus and PFC, we observed a sustained increase in alpha (7–15 Hz) frequency range phase synchrony while Unconscious (p<0.01, cluster-based non-parametric randomization test, Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: Thalamic stimulation increased muscle tone during the Unconscious state.
source: Electrical stimulation of the thalamus increased muscle tone (non-parametric randomization test, p<0.01, Figure 8C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: Thalamic stimulation increased eyeblinks to airpuffs during the Unconscious state.
source: eyeblinks to airpuffs (non-parametric randomization test, p<0.01, Figure 8D)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: Thalamic stimulation increased blood oxygen saturation during the Unconscious state.
source: blood oxygen saturation (non-parametric randomization test, p<0.01, Figure 8E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8E with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: Thalamic stimulation increased heart rate during the Unconscious state.
source: and heart rate (non-parametric randomization test, p<0.01, Figure 8F)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: These changes from thalamic stimulation were all greater for high relative to low-current and outlasted the electrical stimulation period itself.
source: These changes were all greater for high relative to low-current (Figure 8C–F, non-parametric randomization test for significant differences between high- vs. low-current stimulation, p<0.01 are indicated with black stars) and outlasted the electrical stimulation period itself, achieving significance during the time window from 0 to 30 s post stimulation offset (post-stim one in Figure 8C–F) and sometimes the 30–60 s (post-stim 2) or 60–90 s (post-stim 3) post stimulation offset periods.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C–F with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: High-current stimulation increased the spike rate from ~1 to ~2.5 spikes/s.
source: High-current stimulation increased the spike rate (Figure 9B and Figure 9C, upper subpanel) from ~1 to ~2.5 spikes/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9C.

claim: In all areas, there was a significant increase in spiking during the stimulation interval compared to the pre-stimulation Unconscious state.
source: In all areas, there was a significant increase in spiking during the stimulation interval compared to the pre-stimulation Unconscious state (Figure 9C, orange bars in upper subpanel, red stars indicate significant differences, p<0.01, non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: In area STG, the increase in spike rate brought the average spike rate to the same level as that seen during natural ROC.
source: In area STG, this increase brought the average spike rate to the same level as that seen during natural ROC (horizontal dotted lines in Figure 9C, upper subpanel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: In all areas, the increased spike rate persisted for at least 30 s (and as long as 90 s) post-stimulation.
source: In all areas, the increased spike rate persisted for at least 30 s (and as long as 90 s) post-stimulation (Figure 9C, red stars indicate significant differences, p<0.01, non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: With low-current stimulation, mean spikes rates were unchanged from pre-stimulation baseline.
source: With low-current stimulation, mean spikes rates were unchanged from pre-stimulation baseline (Figure 9C, lower subpanel, all p>0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C with statistical analysis (p>0.01).

claim: High-current, but not low-current, stimulation significantly reduced slow-frequency power for up to 85 s post electrical stimulation onset relative to pre-stimulation baseline.
source: High-current, but not low-current, stimulation significantly reduced slow-frequency power for up to 85 s post electrical stimulation onset relative to pre-stimulation baseline (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, p<0.01, cluster-based non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: High-current stimulation decreased within-area spike-LFP slow-frequency synchronization in three of four cortical areas.
source: In addition, high-current stimulation decreased within-area spike-LFP (in three of four cortical areas, Figure 9F) as well as cortico-cortical and thalamo-cortical LFP-LFP slow-frequency synchronization (Figure 9—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: High-current stimulation significantly increased higher-frequency power during and after stimulation.
source: High-current stimulation also significantly increased higher-frequency power during and after stimulation (Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2, p<0.01, cluster-based non-parametric randomization test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and Figure 9—figure supplement 2 with statistical analysis (p<0.01).

claim: During stimulation, the enhancement had a well-defined peak in the alpha-beta band in area 8A and PFC at 13 Hz in 8A and 15 Hz in PFC.
source: During stimulation, the enhancement had a well-defined peak in the alpha-beta band in area 8A and PFC (vertical dotted lines in Figure 9E indicate peaks at 13 Hz in 8A and 15 Hz in PFC).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The alpha-beta peaks were absent in the 0–30 s post-stimulation offset interval.
source: They were absent in the 0–30 s post-stimulation offset interval (Figure 9G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: The reduction in slow frequency power persisted for 85 s post-stimulation.
source: The reduction in slow frequency power persisted for 85 s post-stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 9D.

claim: All of the effects of thalamic stimulation were weak or absent for low-current stimulation.
source: All of the effects were weak or absent for low-current stimulation (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Propofol likely renders unconsciousness by disrupting intracortical and thalamo-cortical communication through decreased spiking and enhanced slow-frequency power/synchrony.
source: In sum, a mechanism through which propofol likely renders unconsciousness is by disrupting intracortical and thalamo-cortical communication through decreased spiking and enhanced slow-frequency power/synchrony.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Propofol-induced unconsciousness leads to low-spiking Down-states and loss of the higher-frequency coherence thought to integrate cortical information.
source: This leads to low-spiking Down-states and loss of the higher-frequency coherence thought to integrate cortical information (Baars et al., 2013; Cimenser et al., 2011; Crick and Koch, 1990; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Dehaene, 2001; Demertzi et al., 2019; Engel et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2013; Purdon et al., 2013; Tononi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to prior research on cortical information integration.

claim: Alpha-beta is the natural resonance frequency of the thalamo-cortical circuit.
source: We propose that alpha-beta is this circuit's natural resonance frequency.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observation that thalamic stimulation enhanced alpha-beta power.

claim: The mechanisms suggested are likely relevant for other anesthetics that target GABA receptors (e.g., sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, barbiturates, and etomidate).
source: Here, we focused on propofol's actions on cortex and thalamus. The mechanisms we suggest are likely relevant for other anesthetics that target GABA receptors (e.g., sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, barbiturates, and etomidate).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the shared mechanism of action of GABA-ergic anesthetics.

claim: Anesthetics that target NMDA antagonists such as ketamine and nitrous oxide have different dynamics and mechanisms.
source: Anesthetics that target NMDA antagonists such as ketamine and nitrous oxide have different dynamics and mechanisms (Akeju et al., 2016; Pavone et al., 2016; Purdon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Akeju et al., 2016; Pavone et al., 2016; Purdon et al., 2015).

claim: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 found less of a contribution of slow frequencies to the unconscious state and less slow-frequency modulation due to thalamic stimulation compared to the current study.
source: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 found less of a contribution of slow frequencies to the unconscious state and less slow-frequency modulation due to thalamic stimulation.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research (Redinbaugh et al., 2020).

claim: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 found decreases in spike rates only in deep cortical layers, whereas the current study found a stronger contribution of slow frequencies and decreases in spiking in all layers (with a stronger decrease in superficial layers).
source: They found decreases in spike rates only in deep cortical layers. We found a stronger contribution of slow frequencies and decreases in spiking in all layers (with a stronger decrease in superficial layers).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research (Redinbaugh et al., 2020).

claim: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 administered ketamine before propofol whereas the current study administered propofol alone.
source: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 administered ketamine before propofol whereas we administered propofol alone.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental methods to prior research (Redinbaugh et al., 2020).

claim: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 compared Awake to Unconscious in separate sessions, whereas the current study studied the transition in and out of consciousness within a session.
source: They compared Awake to Unconscious in separate sessions. We studied the transition in and out of consciousness within a session.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental methods to prior research (Redinbaugh et al., 2020).

claim: Redinbaugh et al., 2020 used a single stimulating linear array centered in the ILN and found that 50 Hz was most effective at inducing arousal from the unconscious state.
source: They used a single stimulating linear array centered in the ILN and found that 50 Hz was most effective at inducing arousal from the unconscious state.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental methods to prior research (Redinbaugh et al., 2020).

claim: The current study used larger stimulating electrode arrays in pairs targeting both ILN and MD, higher currents, and 180 Hz.
source: By contrast, we used larger stimulating electrode arrays in pairs targeting both ILN and MD, higher currents, and 180 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the current study.

claim: The stimulation parameters used in the current study were chosen to approximate stimulation parameters that were effective in increasing arousal in a minimally conscious human.
source: We did so to approximate stimulation parameters that were effective in increasing arousal in a minimally conscious human (Schiff et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental methods based on prior research (Schiff et al., 2007).
